Using global data on the Mean Trophic Level (MTL) between 1950 and 2018 and a comprehensive dataset of environmental provisions from trade agreements signed between 1947 and 2018, we estimate the impact on the MTL of signing (i) a free trade agreement and (ii) a free trade agreement including fishery-related provisions. To address potential endogeneity problems associated with fisheries-related provisions, we use a difference-in-differences (DID) propensity score matching method. Our results show that while trade agreements tend to negatively impact the MTL, including fisheries-related provisions offsets this negative impact among signatory countries. By examining the potential mechanisms underlyingthisresult,weareabletotempertheoptimisticfindingsintheexistingliteratureonthebeneficial environmental outcomes of environmental provisions. Our findings suggest that these provisions do not foster the adoption of more effective resource management practices. Instead, they appear to reduce trade opportunities, which is contrary to the objective of trade creation in trade agreements. Conclusions 681 In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of fishery-related provisions (FRPs) in regional trade agreements 682 (RTAs) in mitigating the decline in the sustainability of fisheries resources that results from trade liberal- 683 ization. As an indicator of the sustainability of fisheries resources, we use the Mean Trophic Level (MTL) 684 (Pauly et al., 1998). This measure has the advantage of having global coverage and being consistent across 685 countries and years, which is crucial for the assessment of the effectiveness of trade agreements on the sus- 686 tainability of fisheries resources. Our empirical strategy addresses the potential endogeneity of the inclusion 687 of FRPs in RTAs. For the 726 RTAs signed during the period 1947-2018, we estimate the impact both of 688 signing a trade agreement and that of the FRPs on the MTL using a difference-in-differences (DID) propen- 689 sity score matching method. Our empirical results thus reflect causal relationships between the inclusion of 690 environmental provision and the MTL. 691 Our empirical results provide interesting insights. First, we find that the average trade agreements reduce 692 the MTL by 1%, while the agreements that include FRPs result in no change in the MTL (compared to the 693 agreementswithouttheseprovisions). JSON: Name: rtas_frp_mtl_did_match Title: Estimating the causal effect of fishery-related provisions in regional trade agreements on marine sustainability using difference-in-differences with propensity-score matching Short Hypothesis: Signing a regional trade agreement that includes at least one fishery-related provision causally reduces the post-signature decline in the Mean Trophic Level of catches among the signatory countries relative to comparable RTAs without such provisions within 5–10 years after implementation. Related Work: Prior empirical work has examined (1) the environmental impacts of non-trade provisions in regional trade agreements using cross-country or agreement-level regressions, (2) the relationship between trade/openness and renewable resource depletion for fisheries, and (3) the design and content of environmental provisions in RTAs. Existing approaches typically rely on two-way fixed effects (TWFE) event-study or cross-sectional comparisons and have identified correlations between environmental clauses and outcomes such as deforestation, air pollution, and emissions. Limitations in prior work include insufficient control for the endogeneity of provision inclusion, limited use of matching or credible counterfactuals, aggregation at donor/recipient levels without agreement-level matching, weak attention to dynamic lagged ecological responses, and limited exploration of mechanisms (trade volume vs. management practice change). Several studies also use coarse provision codings or do not apply heterogeneity-robust estimators to handle staggered treatment timing and multiple agreements per country. Abstract: This research pipeline tests whether fishery-related provisions (FRPs) embedded in regional trade agreements (RTAs) causally affect the sustainability of marine fisheries, measured by the Mean Trophic Level (MTL) of catches. We estimate agreement-level causal effects by combining propensity-score matching of RTAs (to create credible counterfactuals) with difference-in-differences and event-study estimators that allow dynamic treatment effects. The approach uses harmonized catch-reconstruction MTL data, a comprehensive RTA provision database, and country-level controls aggregated to the agreement-year panel. Main contributions are (i) an ex-post causal evaluation design that accounts for selection into FRPs, (ii) heterogeneity-robust dynamic estimators for staggered RTA adoption, and (iii) mechanism tests separating trade-volume and fishing-technology channels (catches, exports, trawling share). Expected outcomes are credible ATT estimates for MTL over 0–15 years post-signature, evidence on timing of effects, and quantification of whether observed ecological changes are driven by trade restriction effects or by improvements in management practices. Experiments: Data: Sea Around Us reconstructed catch data to compute country-year and agreement-year MTL (1950–2018, primary inference restricted to post-1980), TREND provision-level RTA dataset (provision coding and bindingness), DESTA RTA metadata (signatories, signature years), FAO trade flows (fish exports), World Bank GDP and governance indices, IUCN/WDPA marine protected area data, catch-share program indicators, subsidy data. Panel construction: aggregate EEZ MTL to country-year by catch-weighting, then aggregate country-year to agreement-year by country catch-weighting; construct agreement-level covariates (sum/mean of signatories’ GDP, catches, exports, protected area, governance). Propensity modeling: estimate propensity score for an RTA containing >=1 FRP using logit with covariates (number of signatories, signature year polynomials, pre-signature (t-5..t) sums of catches and exports, ln(protected area), share developed signatories, baseline MTL, total land area, biocapacity per capita, prior number of environmental provisions). Matching: primary 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching without replacement with caliper 0.05; robustness: kernel-weighted and 1:3 matching. Balance checks: standardized mean differences <0.1 for all covariates. Estimation: run DID/TWFE with agreement and year fixed effects on matched sample; main regression y_gt = alpha0 + alpha1 PostRTA_gt + alpha2 (PostRTA_gt × FRP_g) + controls + FE. Dynamic/event-study: estimate interaction effects for tau = -15..+15 years relative to signature; implement heterogeneity-robust estimators (Sun & Abraham; Borusyak et al.; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille). Clustering: cluster SEs at agreement level. Baselines: unmatched TWFE DID, matched DID without interaction, placebo outcome (manufactured exports), alternative outcomes (EPI fish stock status, total overexploited catches). Mechanisms: outcome regressions for (log) total catches, (log) fish exports, share of catch by trawl; include identical DID and event-study specifications. Ablation and sensitivity: (a) alternative FRP sets (narrow fish-only, extended environmental), (b) use number of FRPs and bindingness dummies, (c) alternative aggregation weights (production, sqrt catch, unweighted), (d) alternative propensity covariates and calipers, (e) group-specific linear trends and pre-trend falsification (placebo leads). Evaluation metrics: average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) on MTL, dynamic coefficients with 95% CIs, percent change in catches/exports, p-values, balance SMDs, pre-trend joint F-tests (p>0.1 required), robustness across estimators and weighting rules. Identification checks: placebo outcomes (manufacturing exports) must show null effects; long-run effect stability reported for 5–10 and 11–15 year windows. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Residual endogeneity: matching addresses selection on observables but cannot eliminate bias from unobserved confounders that predict both FRP inclusion and post-signature MTL trends. 2) Measurement error: Sea Around Us reconstructed catches and MTL are subject to reporting bias and reconstruction uncertainty that may vary systematically by country and time. 3) Aggregation bias: agreement-level aggregation by catch weights can under- or over-emphasize large signatories and obscure within-country heterogeneity. 4) Limited power and sample truncation: long-run (10+ year) event windows reduce sample size because many RTAs are recent, increasing variance and limiting inference on long-term dynamics. 5) TWFE heterogeneity bias: staggered timing and multiple treatments per country can bias standard TWFE estimates; heterogeneity-robust estimators mitigate but do not remove all concerns. 6) Mechanism identification: distinguishing whether impacts arise from trade-restrictive effects versus improved management requires stronger instruments or micro-level policy timing and may remain inconclusive. 7) Provision coding error: misclassification of FRP content or bindingness in TREND can attenuate estimated effects. 8) External validity: results apply to RTAs and the studied period and may not generalize to unilateral trade liberalization or to freshwater and terrestrial resources. 9) Computational constraints: repeated matching and heterogeneity-robust estimators with multiple sensitivity analyses require substantial computation and careful reproducibility controls.
